questions.q_en:
Renewable energy is often presented as an uncomplicated remedy to the twin crises of climate change and energy insecurity. Governments announce ambitious targets, corporations highlight sustainability commitments, and public discourse treats renewables as an inevitable successor to fossil fuels. Yet this narrative of inevitability conceals a more complex reality. Transitioning to renewable energy is not merely a technological substitution but a structural transformation involving land use, grid stability, economic redistribution, and political negotiation. Ignoring these dimensions risks replacing one form of dependency with another. One persistent challenge lies in intermittency. Solar and wind energy, while abundant, are not continuously available, requiring storage systems or backup infrastructure. Although technological advances have reduced costs, large-scale storage remains economically and logistically constrained. As a result, renewable integration often relies on conventional energy sources during periods of low generation. This dependence complicates claims of energy independence and exposes the limits of viewing renewables as a standalone solution.

Social and environmental trade-offs further complicate the transition. Large renewable projects demand vast land areas, sometimes displacing communities or disrupting local ecosystems. Ironically, projects designed to mitigate environmental harm can generate localized ecological and social resistance. When decision-making excludes affected populations, renewable energy risks replicating the extractive logic historically associated with fossil fuels—only under a different moral banner.

The long-term success of renewable energy, therefore, depends less on technological optimism and more on institutional capacity. Transparent governance, adaptive grid management, and equitable distribution of costs and benefits are critical. Without these, renewable energy may expand in capacity yet fall short in legitimacy, provoking resistance that slows the very transition it seeks to accelerate.

“Ignoring these dimensions risks replacing one form of dependency with another,”
the phrase “replacing one form of dependency with another” functions as:

questions.q_en:
In the sentence below, identify the type of conjunction used in “not only...but also”:

The researcher not only published groundbreaking studies in international journals but also mentored several young scientists during her career.
questions.q_hi:
In the sentence below, identify the type of conjunction used in “not only...but also”:

The researcher not only published groundbreaking studies in international journals but also mentored several young scientists during her career.
questions.solution_en:
Answer: B) Correlative Conjunction

Explanation: Correlative conjunctions are pairs of conjunctions that work together to connect equal words, phrases, or clauses.

Common examples include:

either...or

neither...nor

not only...but also

Here, “not only...but also” connects two related actions:

  1. published groundbreaking studies

  2. mentored several young scientists

Therefore, it is a correlative conjunction.

questions.q_hi:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.

She said to him, "Did you visit the museum yesterday?"
options_en: She asked him whether he had visited the museum the previous day.
She asked him if he visited the museum the previous day.
She asked him whether he had visited the museum yesterday.
She told him if he had visited the museum the previous day.
options_hi: She asked him whether he had visited the museum the previous day.

questions.solution_en:
The correct answer is Option A: She asked him whether he had visited the museum the previous day.

Key Points

  • Reporting Verb Change: In this Direct Speech sentence, there is a reporting verb with an object ("said to him"), so "said to" changes to "asked".

  • Conjunction: We remove commas and inverted commas. For "Yes/No" questions starting with auxiliary verbs like "Did," the conjunction "if" or "whether" is added.

  • Tense Shift: The sentence is in the Simple Past ("Did... visit"). When converting to Indirect Speech, the Simple Past changes to the Past Perfect ("had visited").

  • Pronoun Change: The second-person pronoun "you" changes according to the object of the reporting verb ("him"), becoming "he".

  • Time Expression: The word "yesterday" changes to "the previous day" or "the day before".

  • Sentence Structure: The interrogative form ("Did you visit") is changed into an assertive form ("he had visited") in Indirect Speech.

questions.q_hi:

options_en: shout for / shout at
shout at / shout for
shout for / shout for
shout at / shout at
options_hi: shout for / shout at
shout at / shout for
shout for / shout for
shout at / shout at
questions.solution_en:
Rule / Concept: Shout at vs. Shout for

In English grammar, the preposition following "shout" significantly alters the intent of the action:

Application to the Given Question

"...began to shout for help when he spotted a rescue helicopter, but he later had to shout at his companion for ignoring the safety protocols..."

In the first blank, the hiker is calling out to obtain "help" (a request/need), which requires "for". In the second blank, he is expressing anger toward his "companion" (the target of his frustration), which requires "at".

Things to Remember / Exam Tips

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: During his tenure as the Chief Justice, he usually
arrived at the court exactly at ten o'clock
every morning regardless of the weather conditions.
No Error
options_hi: During his tenure as the Chief Justice, he usually
arrived at the court exactly at ten o'clock
every morning regardless of the weather conditions.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (D) - No Error.

📌 Rule / Concept: Simple Past for Discontinued Habits vs. General Habits -

Simple Present (V1/V1+s) is used for habits that are currently true or part of a regular routine. However, the Simple Past (V2) is used to describe habits or routines that were true in the past but are no longer happening.

When a sentence provides a specific past time context (such as "During his tenure," "When I was a child," or "Last year"), the use of V2 with frequency adverbs like "usually" or "every day" is perfectly correct. It indicates a Past Habit.

PAST HABIT: V2 + Daily/Every day

💢 Application to the Given Question - The phrase "During his tenure" sets a clear boundary in the past. It tells us that the person is likely no longer the Chief Justice or that we are specifically discussing a historical period of his life. Because the context is firmly rooted in the past, the verb "arrived" (Simple Past) is correctly used to describe his routine during that specific time.

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1 ✅: When I was in school, I visited the library every day. (Past habit)

Example 2 ✅: My grandfather always smoked a pipe after dinner. (A habit of someone who is no longer here or has quit)

Example 3 ✅: She usually walked to work when she lived in London. (Context of living in London is past)

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: While wandering through the ancient
ruins of Rome, a sudden thunderstorm
caught the tourists off guard.
options_hi: While wandering through the ancient
ruins of Rome, a sudden thunderstorm
caught the tourists off guard.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A) Replace “While wandering” with “While the tourists were wandering”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Misrelated or Dangling Participles

A participle is a verb acting as an adjective. When a sentence begins with a participle phrase (e.g., Walking..., Wandering..., Being...), the noun or pronoun immediately following the comma must be the logical doer of that action. If the subject following the comma cannot perform the action, the participle is "dangling" or "misrelated."

💢 Application to the Given Question

While wandering through the ancient (A)/ ruins of Rome, a sudden (B)/ thunderstorm caught the tourists... (C)

In this sentence, the subject following the comma is "a sudden thunderstorm." Grammatically, this implies that the thunderstorm was wandering through the ancient ruins. Since a thunderstorm cannot "wander," the participle is dangling. To fix this, we must provide a logical subject for the wandering (the tourists) within the first part.

Corrected Sentence

While the tourists were wandering through the ancient ruins of Rome, a sudden thunderstorm caught them off guard.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: The temperature dropped from
as low as five degrees
during the long winter night.
No Error
options_hi: The temperature dropped from
as low as five degrees
during the long winter night.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option A

👉 Replace “from” with “to”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Verbs of Movement vs. Range Constructions

In English grammar, the choice of preposition depends on whether you are establishing a range (starting and ending points) or a destination/result of an action.

To: Used after verbs of change or movement (like dropped, fell, rose, increased) to indicate the final result or the point reached.

From... to: Used only when both the starting point and the ending point are explicitly mentioned in the sentence.

As... as: This is a degree modifier used for emphasis (e.g., as low as).

💢 Application to the Given Question

(The temperature dropped from / as low as five degrees / during the long winter night.)

In this sentence, the verb "dropped" describes a downward movement. The phrase "five degrees" represents the final level reached by the temperature, not the starting point. If you use "from," the sentence implies that five degrees was the temperature before it dropped, which contradicts the context. Therefore, "to" is required to show the resulting low temperature.

✅ Corrected Sentence

The temperature dropped to as low as five degrees during the long winter night.

During the annual cultural festival held at the university last year, every boy and every girl _______ present to witness the spectacular performance.
questions.q_hi:
The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar.

During the annual cultural festival held at the university last year, every boy and every girl _______ present to witness the spectacular performance.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (C)- The blank should be filled with the singular past tense verb "was".

Rule 1: The "Each/Every" Rule (Subject-Verb Agreement) Even when multiple nouns are joined by "and," if they are preceded by "each" or "every," the entire subject is treated as singular. This is because the focus is on every individual person separately.

Incorrect: Every boy and girl were...

Correct: Every boy and girl was/is...

Rule 2: Tense Consistency (Time Markers) In competitive exams, once you identify the subject is singular, you must check the time marker to choose between "is" and "was."

The sentence contains the phrase "last year."

"Last year" indicates a completed action in the past (Simple Past Tense).

Therefore, the singular present verb "is" is incorrect, and the singular past verb "was" must be used.

Correct Sentence: ...every boy and every girl was present to witness the spectacular performance.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (C). Both "All is well" and "All are well" are grammatically correct, but they carry different meanings based on the context.

Rule/Concept: "All" as an Indefinite Pronoun The word "All" is treated as singular when it refers to a non-countable concept or a general situation. It is treated as plural when it refers to countable people or things.

Logic Breakdown:

"All is well" (Option A): In this case, "All" refers to a general condition, state of affairs, or everything as a whole (Uncountable).

Example: Everything in life is going fine. (All is well).

"All are well" (Option B): Here, "All" refers to specific individuals or members of a group, such as family members or friends (Countable).

Example: All the people in my family are doing fine. (All are well).

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option D

👉 The blanks should be filled with “so” and “that”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Cause and Effect (So... that)

The pair "So... that" is a correlative conjunction used to show how the intensity of a quality (the cause) leads to a specific result (the effect).

Structure: So + Adjective/Adverb + that + Resulting Clause.

The Difference from "Too... to": * So... that is followed by a complete clause (Subject + Verb).

Too... to is followed by an infinitive verb (V1).

✅ Correct Sentence

questions.solution_en:

Rule/Concept: Collective Nouns (Division of Opinion) Normally, a collective noun (like jury, committee, team, family) takes a singular verb when the group acts as one unit. However, if the members are divided, have different opinions, or are acting individually, the noun is treated as plural.

Logic Breakdown:

The "Division" Clue: Segment (B) uses the word "divided" and segment (C) uses "opinions" (plural). This proves the members are not acting as a single unit.

The Pronoun Clue: Segment (B) uses the plural possessive pronoun "their." A singular subject ("was") cannot be paired with a plural pronoun ("their") in the same sentence.

The Conflict: To maintain consistency with "divided" and "their," the verb in segment (A) must be plural (were).

Corrected Sentence: The jury were divided in their opinions regarding the verdict.

questions.q_en: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.
questions.q_hi: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.
options_en: Two-thirds of the modern laboratory equipments were broken.
The variety of rare postage stamps were lost.
No worker and no senior clerk was present.
Most of the private digital information were leaked.
options_hi: Two-thirds of the modern laboratory equipments were broken.
The variety of rare postage stamps were lost.
No worker and no senior clerk was present.
Most of the private digital information were leaked.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (C)- This is the only sentence that adheres to the rules of Subject-Verb Agreement.

Logic Breakdown:

(A) Two-thirds of the modern laboratory equipments were broken:

Error: The noun following "of" is "equipment," which is uncountable. Uncountable nouns (like water, milk, or equipment) always require a singular verb.

Correction: ...equipment was broken.

Equipment doesn’t take ‘s’.

(B) The variety of rare postage stamps were lost:

Error: The phrase "The variety of" focuses on the single group or selection. It must always take a singular verb. (Recall: "A variety" would take "were").

Correction: The variety... was lost.

(C) No worker and no senior clerk was present:

Status: CORRECT. When two singular nouns are joined by "and" but are both preceded by the word "No," the subject is treated as singular (0 + 0 = 0). The singular verb "was" is perfectly correct.

(D) Most of the private digital information were leaked:

Error: The noun following "of" is "information," which is uncountable. Just like equipment, it cannot be pluralized and must take a singular verb.

Correction: ...information was leaked.

questions.q_en:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.

Rutu said to her brother, "If I were you, I would always come here while the sun was setting."
questions.q_hi:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.

Rutu said to her brother, "If I were you, I would always come here while the sun was setting."
options_en: Rutu told her brother that if she was him, she would always go there while the sun was setting.
Rutu advised her brother that if she was him, she would always go there while the sun had been setting.
Rutu told her brother that if she had been him, she would have always gone there while the sun was setting.
Rutu advised her brother that if she were him, she would always go there while the sun was setting.
options_hi: Rutu told her brother that if she was him, she would always go there while the sun was setting.
Rutu advised her brother that if she was him, she would always go there while the sun had been setting.
Rutu told her brother that if she had been him, she would have always gone there while the sun was setting.
Rutu advised her brother that if she were him, she would always go there while the sun was setting.
questions.solution_en:
The correct answer is Option D: Rutu advised her brother that if she were him, she would always go there while the sun was setting.

Key Points:

  • The "Advice" Verb: Since "If I were you" is a standard way of offering a suggestion, the reporting verb "advised" is more contextually accurate than "said" or "told."

  • The Subjunctive "Were": In hypothetical conditions ("If I were..."), the word "were" is preserved in indirect speech. It does not change to "was" or "had been".

  • The Simultaneous Action Exception: This is the biggest trap. Rules for past habits or actions happening at the same time (connected by "while") dictate that the tense does not change. Therefore, "was setting" stays exactly as "was setting".

  • The Place Shift: The word "here" must change to "there" to reflect the change in perspective.

Breaking Down the Incorrect Options:

  • Option A: Incorrectly changes the subjunctive "were" to "was" and uses the weaker reporting verb "told."

  • Option B: falls for the common trap of shifting a simultaneous action into the past perfect ("had been setting"), which is grammatically incorrect for parallel past events.

  • Option C: Incorrectly treats the hypothetical scenario as a completed past fact by using "had been... would have gone."
